strengths: The paper tackles a challenging and relevant vision problem: reconstructing rapidly changing, emissive, partially transparent flames from only three consumer cameras. Integrating capture, synchronization, background reconstruction, and dynamic Gaussian modeling is practically valuable.

The reported flame-region results are promising. Across 17 scenes, the method achieves 27.46 dB PSNR and 0.8469 SSIM, compared with 25.51 dB and 0.8019 for the stronger 4DGS baseline. Figure 9 also shows better preservation of flame details in several examples.

The ablations support separating static and dynamic reconstruction and indicate benefits from flow initialization, particularly for flame SSIM. Per-scene results and explicit reporting of the competitor's better full-frame metrics improve transparency.

The supplementary material provides implementation and hardware details, reports approximately 30-minute training and 131 Hz rendering, and describes an intended code and dataset release. The discussion appropriately acknowledges limitations of optical flow, linear trajectories, and static-background assumptions.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central novel-view and 3D reconstruction claims. Section 5 holds out every eighth frame from the same three cameras, primarily testing temporal interpolation at observed viewpoints. Qualitative novel-view trajectories described in the supplement lack corresponding reference images. A held-out camera or controlled synthetic experiment would provide substantially stronger evidence of spatial generalization. Furthermore, each reconstruction uses only 100 frames at 400 Hz, approximately 0.25 seconds, despite the longer captured sequences.

The depth metric is not independent evidence of geometric accuracy. The method explicitly initializes and regularizes its background using DepthAnythingV2, then evaluates depth against aligned predictions from that same estimator. The baselines do not receive equivalent supervision. This favors agreement with the chosen prior and cannot establish correct flame geometry, especially because Figure 9 itself notes that monocular depth misses transparent flame regions. The claimed spatial degeneration of competing methods therefore needs stronger validation than this metric alone.

The central flow-fusion formulation lacks a sound projection derivation. Equation (6) supplies only one scalar constraint per camera, whereas optical flow has two components. It constrains displacement along the observed flow direction but does not enforce the perpendicular image-motion component; a zero-flow observation supplies no constraint at all. Moreover, fixed-depth back-projection does not generally justify this equality for perspective motion with changing depth. Equation (8) consequently does not ensure reprojection consistency. A derivation using camera projection geometry, or validation against known 3D motion, is needed.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed algorithmic contribution sufficiently. Both 4DGS baselines use random initialization and settings taken from the flame-salmon scene, whereas the proposed method receives substantial geometry initialization and static-scene preprocessing. FreeTimeGS, whose lifetime and linear-velocity representation is directly adopted, is not evaluated as a matched baseline. Comparing methods with equivalent initialization and background treatment would clarify how much improvement comes specifically from the proposed flow fusion.

Evidence for the claimed importance of precise timing is limited. Removing rolling-shutter modeling leaves performance effectively unchanged, and introducing offsets of up to one frame reduces flame PSNR by only 0.34 dB. These results do not invalidate the synchronization hardware, but they do not establish that microsecond precision is necessary for the demonstrated reconstructions. The approximately 15-microsecond precision is estimated from row timing and edge-localization assumptions rather than independently measured synchronization error.

Several details needed to reproduce and interpret the method remain unclear in the manuscript: voxel-grid bounds and resolution, the regularization coefficient in flow fusion, dynamic-mask construction, displacement-to-velocity conversion, and the precise dynamic training objective. Equations (3) and (4) also include the depth weight twice. The evaluation should specify whether held-out images are excluded from optical-flow estimation and other preprocessing. Although the supplement describes accompanying code, these ambiguities remain unresolved in the supplied PDF.

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and relevant vision problem: reconstructing rapidly changing, emissive flames from only three consumer cameras. Integrating background reconstruction, dynamic Gaussians, flow initialization, and visual synchronization is a useful practical direction.

The experiments cover 17 real scenes with multiple fuels and flame conditions. Table 1 reports meaningful improvements in flame-region reconstruction over the stronger Yang et al. baseline: PSNR increases from 25.51 to 27.46 dB and SSIM from 0.8019 to 0.8469. Figure 9 also shows convincing examples of recovered flame detail.

The component ablations and supplementary per-scene results provide useful transparency. Separating static and dynamic optimization substantially improves flame-region PSNR, while flow initialization improves average flame-region SSIM.

The manuscript attributes its FreeTimeGS representation and other building blocks, reports training and rendering costs, and acknowledges limitations involving optical flow, linear motion, and background interactions. The synchronization hardware and planned dataset release could be useful community resources.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central claim of accurate sparse-view 3D reconstruction. Section 5 holds out every eighth frame from the same camera viewpoints, testing temporal interpolation rather than novel-view accuracy. Supplementary novel-view trajectories are described, but there is no quantitative held-out-camera evaluation or independent geometry/motion reference. Moreover, each reconstructed sequence contains only 100 frames at 400 Hz, approximately 0.25 seconds, limiting evidence for sustained temporal coherence.

The depth evaluation is not independent of the method's priors. The proposed system uses aligned DepthAnythingV2 predictions for background initialization and strong depth regularization, then evaluates rendered depth against aligned monocular predictions. This measures agreement with the prior rather than verified geometry, and favors the proposed pipeline over baselines without that supervision. Figure 9 suggests baseline artifacts, but the reported depth-error gap cannot establish accurate flame geometry or physically plausible motion.

The central flow-fusion formulation is insufficiently justified. Equation (6), (F − u_i)^T u_i = 0, constrains only the component along the lifted optical-flow vector; it does not enforce the full two-dimensional reprojection constraint. Even under an orthographic approximation, motion perpendicular to the observed flow can remain unconstrained, and zero observed flow contributes no constraint. Perspective projection introduces additional dependence on motion along the viewing direction. The paper needs a derivation or controlled validation explaining why this approximation provides reliable 3D initialization.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution beyond the adopted FreeTimeGS representation and stronger preprocessing. Both 4DGS baselines receive random initialization and existing flame-salmon settings, whereas the proposed method receives stereo/monocular geometry, separate background fitting, and flow initialization. There is no direct FreeTimeGS comparison under matched conditions or baseline equipped with comparable geometry priors. This matters because Yang et al. performs better on all three full-frame appearance metrics. The results support flame-region gains, but not an unqualified reconstruction advantage.

Evidence for some highlighted components is limited. Removing rolling-shutter modeling produces essentially unchanged, slightly higher flame metrics, and the artificial synchronization perturbation reduces flame PSNR by only 0.34 dB. The claimed approximately 15-microsecond synchronization precision is estimated from row timing and edge localization rather than independently measured. Flow initialization contributes 0.45 dB on average and has mixed per-scene effects. These results warrant narrower claims about the necessity and demonstrated benefits of the capture and initialization components.

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and useful computer-vision problem: reconstructing rapidly changing, semi-transparent flames from only three consumer cameras. Integrating capture synchronization, background reconstruction, and dynamic Gaussian modeling is a meaningful practical contribution.

The evaluation includes 17 real scenes with different fuels and flame characteristics. Table 1 reports clear improvements in flame-region quality over both tested baselines: 27.46 dB PSNR and 0.8469 SSIM, compared with 25.51 dB and 0.8019 for the stronger baseline.

The ablations support separating static and dynamic reconstruction: removing static pretraining reduces flame PSNR by 3.14 dB. Flow initialization also improves average flame quality, particularly SSIM.

The manuscript credits its FreeTimeGS-based representation and other borrowed components, discusses relevant limitations candidly, and provides supplementary implementation details, per-scene results, and resource measurements. The reported approximately 30-minute training and real-time rendering are practically attractive.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central claim of accurate sparse-view 3D reconstruction. Section 5 holds out every eighth frame from the same three cameras, primarily measuring temporal interpolation at observed viewpoints. Qualitative novel-view trajectories are described, but there is no quantitative evaluation against an unseen camera. Furthermore, each reconstruction uses only 100 frames at 400 Hz—approximately 0.25 seconds—so sustained temporal coherence remains untested.

The depth evaluation is not independent evidence of geometric accuracy. RMSEdepth measures agreement with aligned monocular predictions from the same depth-estimation method used for initialization and strong background regularization. This favors the proposed pipeline and cannot establish correct flame geometry, especially for transparent volumes without a unique surface depth. The large depth-score advantage therefore does not justify the manuscript's stronger conclusions about spatial or physical correctness.

The central flow-fusion formulation needs a sound derivation or correction. Equation 6 supplies only one scalar constraint per camera and does not enforce the complete two-dimensional flow observation. For perspective cameras, it is not generally equivalent to requiring that projecting x + F reproduce the observed displacement. Equation 8 consequently estimates a heuristic field whose geometric validity is unestablished. This matters because explicit, interpretable 3D motion is a stated contribution.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution sufficiently. Both 4DGS baselines receive random initialization, whereas the proposed method receives stereo geometry, monocular depth regularization, a separately trained background, and optical-flow initialization. A comparison with the closest underlying method, FreeTimeGS, under matched preprocessing is missing. RandFlow helps isolate velocity initialization, but its average gain is only 0.45 dB and is inconsistent across scenes. Stronger controlled comparisons are needed to attribute the improvement.

The evidence for the synchronization and high-frequency claims is limited. Removing rolling-shutter modeling leaves the metrics essentially unchanged, and introducing a one-frame timing offset reduces flame PSNR by only 0.34 dB. The approximately 15-microsecond precision is inferred from row timing and assumed localization accuracy rather than independently measured. These results support a useful capture design, but do not establish its claimed necessity or precise accuracy.

Several details needed to reproduce the new component are unspecified in the manuscript, including voxel-grid construction, the regularization constant, dynamic-mask generation, and how preprocessing excludes held-out observations. Although the supplement states that code is included, these details should also be made explicit. Overall, the promising image-quality results do not yet resolve the methodological and validation concerns surrounding the main 3D reconstruction claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and relevant problem: reconstructing rapidly changing, semi-transparent flames from three consumer cameras. The combination of background reconstruction, flow initialization, and dynamic Gaussians is practically motivated.

The reported appearance improvements are substantial across 17 real scenes. Table 1 shows flame PSNR of 26.93 dB versus 24.48 dB for the strongest baseline on this metric, and flame SSIM of 0.843 versus 0.756. Figure 5 also shows sharper flame structure and fewer background artifacts.

The evaluation goes beyond image similarity by including video quality and synthetic velocity measurements. Table 2 reports substantially better directional alignment with simulated flow, and the RandFlow ablation supports the importance of motion initialization.

The consumer-camera synchronization setup and diverse captured fuels are useful practical contributions. The supplement provides implementation and hardware details, credits the synthetic scene assets, and discusses meaningful limitations involving optical flow, linear motion, and smoke.
weaknesses: The central flow-fusion derivation is not justified as a valid perspective projection constraint. Equation (4) imposes only one scalar constraint per camera, whereas an observed image displacement ordinarily supplies two. Moreover, back-projecting the displaced pixel at the original depth does not generally make the residual true displacement orthogonal to the resulting vector u_i. Zero observed flow contributes no constraint at all in Equation (6), although it should constrain transverse motion. The authors should derive the appropriate camera projection constraints or explicitly justify this formulation as a heuristic and compare it with geometrically consistent flow triangulation.

The evidence does not adequately establish novel-view reconstruction or accurate flame geometry. Quantitative validation holds out every eighth frame from the same cameras, testing temporal interpolation rather than unseen viewpoints. Novel-view trajectories are described only qualitatively. RMSEdepth measures agreement with linearly aligned monocular predictions, which are not ground-truth depth for translucent flames; the method also uses the same depth-prediction family as a reconstruction prior. Synthetic held-out cameras and independent volumetric or depth measurements would better support the central 3D claims.

The representation-level novelty and explanation of baseline failures are overstated. Section 3.2 explicitly adopts the lifetime and constant-velocity representation from FreeTimeGS, and Appendix H describes adding these parameters similarly to that method. This weakens the introduction's assertion that existing approaches fundamentally assume persistent primitives and that transient temporal support is the distinguishing advance. The potentially valuable contribution is the fire-specific pipeline, but its benefit should be isolated through a controlled FreeTimeGS comparison with matched initialization, background treatment, and supervision.

Baseline comparisons confound representation quality with preprocessing and implementation differences. Most baselines receive COLMAP points and flame-salmon configurations, whereas the proposed method receives dense stereo/monocular initialization, explicit background separation, and optical-flow initialization. FreeTimeGS uses an unofficial implementation whose correspondence initialization demonstrably fails on flames. These experiments establish an advantage over the tested pipelines, but do not establish the claimed fundamental inadequacy of existing dynamic Gaussian representations. Excluding specialized volumetric reconstruction methods on efficiency grounds is also insufficiently supported without a measured quality–runtime comparison.

The physical-motion evidence needs stronger controls. DVE samples and weights locations according to each method's own reconstructed Gaussians, so different methods are evaluated over different spatial support; missing difficult regions is not explicitly penalized. There is no initialization-only velocity baseline to show how much optimization improves the fused flow, especially given the reduced velocity learning rate. The reported relative L2 error of 0.825 still leaves substantial error, and the three synthetic scenes do not establish physically accurate motion on real flames.

Several claims exceed the ablation evidence, and important reproducibility details remain unclear. NoSync changes flame PSNR by only 0.04 dB and leaves several metrics essentially unchanged, providing little support for the necessity of microsecond synchronization. Real-scene experiments use only 100 frames, approximately 0.25 seconds, despite capturing 15-second sequences. The manuscript does not specify the voxel-grid bounds/resolution, regularization strength tau_0, motion-mask construction, or whether held-out frames are excluded from flow and other preprocessing. Appendix I also leaves the repository address blank. These omissions hinder reproduction and assessment of the validation protocol.

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and relevant vision problem: reconstructing transient, emissive flames from only three cameras. The integration of background reconstruction, flow initialization, and dynamic Gaussians has practical value even without a fundamentally new rendering representation.

The reported appearance improvements are substantial. Across 17 real scenes, Table 1 reports flame PSNR of 26.93 dB versus 24.48 dB for the strongest baseline on this metric, with improvements in SSIM and full-frame perceptual quality. Figure 5 provides qualitative support, and the supplementary video-quality metric adds temporal evidence.

Synthetic experiments evaluate motion against simulation velocities rather than relying exclusively on image similarity. Table 2 shows substantially stronger directional alignment, and the RandFlow ablation supports the importance of motion initialization.

The consumer-camera capture setup is useful, and the manuscript provides dataset descriptions, implementation details, and runtime measurements. The discussion appropriately acknowledges limitations involving optical flow, linear motion, smoke, and background interactions.
weaknesses: The flow-fusion formulation has an unresolved technical problem. Equation (4) imposes only one scalar constraint per camera, whereas matching an observed 2D displacement generally imposes two. It does not constrain the component perpendicular to the observed flow, and a zero-flow observation contributes no constraint at all. Under perspective projection, the claimed orthogonality also does not generally follow from back-projecting the displaced pixel at the original depth. Consequently, Equation (6) is not established as geometrically consistent multi-view flow recovery. This central component needs a correct derivation or explicit justification as a heuristic.

The quantitative protocol does not establish the claimed novel-view reconstruction quality. Every eighth frame is withheld from the same three camera viewpoints, primarily testing temporal interpolation. The supplementary novel-view trajectories offer qualitative evidence but no held-out-view reference comparison. Synthetic scenes could provide this directly. Furthermore, the real experiments use only 100 frames per camera, approximately 0.25 seconds at 400 Hz, substantially limiting evidence for sustained temporal reconstruction.

The depth evaluation measures agreement with a monocular predictor, not geometric accuracy. Depth Anything V2 also supplies the method's background initialization and regularization, so this reference is not independent of the method's priors. For semi-transparent flames, the meaning of a single predicted depth is itself unclear. The reported RMSE therefore cannot substantiate the strong claims about accurate flame geometry or establish that competing reconstructions are geometrically incorrect.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed representation from advantages in initialization and supervision. Most baselines receive COLMAP points, whereas the proposed method receives dense stereo/monocular initialization, background separation, and optical-flow initialization. FreeTimeGS uses an unofficial implementation with a different correspondence pipeline. Controlled experiments providing comparable initialization and decomposition to the closest baselines are needed. Excluding all non-GS volumetric methods on efficiency grounds is also insufficiently supported without comparative runtime or quality–cost measurements.

The representational novelty is overstated. Section 3.2 and Appendix H explicitly adopt the lifetime and linear-velocity parameterization from FreeTimeGS, yet the introduction presents transient primitives as the decisive conceptual departure from existing methods. The defensible contribution is the fire-specific reconstruction pipeline; stronger controlled evidence is needed to establish its advance over closely related transient Gaussian methods.

The physical-motion evidence remains limited. DVE samples and weights errors using each method's own reconstructed Gaussians, so different methods are evaluated over different spatial support and can omit difficult regions without a corresponding coverage penalty. The proposed method's relative velocity error remains 0.825. An initialization-only result and evaluation over common ground-truth support would clarify how much optimization recovers beyond the optical-flow prior. The synchronization ablation also produces nearly unchanged real-image scores, providing little support for claims that the custom timing precision is essential.

Several reproduction-critical details are missing or unclear: voxel bounds and resolution, the regularization constant τ0, motion-mask construction, and whether held-out frames are excluded before flow estimation and initialization. Appendix I contains an empty repository reference. These gaps matter because initialization and preprocessing appear central to the reported gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging and relevant vision problem: reconstructing transient, semi-transparent flames from three cameras. The combination of static-background reconstruction, flow initialization, and short-lived dynamic Gaussians is practically motivated.

The reported appearance improvements are substantial across 17 real scenes. In Table 1, flame PSNR reaches 26.93 dB versus 24.48 dB for the strongest baseline on that metric, while full-image LPIPS improves to 0.035 versus 0.053. Figures 5 and 11 support improvements in flame detail and background stability.

The synthetic evaluation goes beyond image similarity by comparing reconstructed velocities with simulation ground truth. Table 2 reports substantially better directional alignment, and the RandFlow ablation provides useful evidence that flow initialization contributes to motion recovery.

The consumer-camera capture setup, synchronization hardware, and reported rendering speed make the system potentially useful. The supplement provides training details and scene descriptions, appropriately attributes synthetic assets, and discusses meaningful limitations involving optical flow, smoke, and background interactions.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish the central novel-view reconstruction claim. Section 5 holds out every eighth frame from the same three cameras, primarily testing temporal interpolation at observed viewpoints. Novel-view trajectories are described qualitatively, without held-out-camera ground truth. Additional synthetic cameras could provide a direct test. Furthermore, the real experiments reconstruct only 100-frame subsequences, approximately 0.25 seconds at 400 Hz, so the 15-second captures do not establish sustained reconstruction quality.

The geometric justification of the flow initialization is problematic. Equation (4) supplies only one scalar constraint per camera, whereas matching a measured 2D flow generally requires two projection constraints. Even under orthographic projection, it leaves the image-plane component perpendicular to the observed flow unconstrained; under perspective projection, the stated dot-product relation does not generally follow from fixed-depth back-projection. Equation (6) therefore needs a justified approximation or comparison with an objective that explicitly matches projected motion. This matters because flow fusion is a central technical contribution.

The claimed representational novelty is overstated. Section 3.2 explicitly adopts FreeTimeGS-style linear velocity and Gaussian temporal opacity, and the supplement again acknowledges this connection. This weakens the introduction's claim that existing methods uniformly assume persistent primitives and that transient primitives are the key new representation. The contribution appears primarily to be the decomposition, initialization, and optimization pipeline. Controlled comparisons that give a close baseline the same background reconstruction, flow initialization, and masks are needed to isolate that contribution.

The depth results measure agreement with a monocular predictor, not geometric accuracy. The method also uses Depth Anything V2 for static-depth regularization, making this evaluation partly aligned with its own prior. For transparent, emissive flames, the intended definition of depth also requires clarification. Consequently, RMSEdepth and the displayed depth maps do not substantiate strong claims of accurate flame geometry. The synthetic motion results are useful but still show relative L2 error of 0.825; moreover, DVE weights and samples each method's own predicted Gaussians, without independently assessing coverage of the ground-truth flame volume.

Several claimed component benefits exceed the ablation evidence. NoSync changes flame PSNR by only 0.04 dB and leaves several metrics effectively unchanged, providing little evidence that the proposed microsecond synchronization is necessary in the tested regime. JointOpt slightly improves synthetic velocity metrics, while NoMask improves appearance. These tradeoffs are partly acknowledged, but the stronger claims about synchronization and physical accuracy need qualification. A flow-initialization-only velocity result would also clarify how much motion accuracy is gained through reconstruction optimization.

Reproducibility and comparison details remain incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly specify motion-mask construction, voxel-grid bounds and resolution, the regularization constant, or whether held-out frames are excluded from optical-flow and other preprocessing. The closest baseline uses an unofficial implementation and different initialization. Restricting evaluation to Gaussian methods is understandable for an efficiency-focused system, but there is no comparative runtime study supporting exclusion of specialized volumetric reconstruction methods. Section I also contains no repository address, although future release is promised.
